Power of Mental Imagery is the fifth volume in a twelve-volume efficiency course. It builds directly on the preceding volume, The Trained Memory. That volume taught that memory works through four elements working together.

The four elements are Retention, Recall, Recognition, and Imagination. Two of them, Retention and Recall, were explained in that earlier book. This fifth volume takes up imagination's share in the process. Mental imagery, it argues, can be trained like a muscle. Readers were promised greater efficiency in business and study. The course belonged to the era's faith in mental training systems. It preserves mail-order self-improvement in its most confident form.

H. Rider Haggard wrote this account of the Salvation Army's social work in Great Britain in 1910, and dedicated it to the Army's officers and soldiers. He praises their self-sacrificing work for the poor and wretched throughout the world. A portrait of General Booth fronts the book.

The contents map men's social work in London: the Spa Road elevator, the Great Peter Street shelter, and a free breakfast service. Work with ex-criminals, a men's workshop in Hanbury Street, Whitechapel, and Sturge House on Bow Road follow. A central labour bureau and an international investigation department close the list, showing aid joined with training and jobs.
